item.content:encoded:
This wave of AI revenue is almost entirely supported by 30 million programmers as heavy users; enterprise penetration is below 5%; once it spreads to 1.5 billion knowledge workers, the market could grow dozens of times larger.

David George connects AI, autonomous driving, legal tech, and VC funding cycles into one cohesive picture, packed with data and virtually no filler.

3:13 Nearly all enterprise AI revenue depends on just 30 million programmers
While the world has 1.5 billion knowledge workers, the vast majority of enterprise AI revenue comes from a single group of just 30 million—programmers. Even within that 30 million, there's an extreme power law: roughly 1 million at the top drive most of the spending. David George sees this as proof the opportunity is huge: penetration today is still microscopic. Once it spreads to a broader base of knowledge workers, the market will dwarf today's size.

4:14 Enterprise penetration below 5% while supply is already booked through 2028
Except for coding and writing, AI's spread through enterprises remains early-stage. Law is an exception—roughly 12 months behind coding, but overall penetration into the knowledge-work market is below 5%. Supply-side pressure is tighter still: new data-center capacity is booked through 2028, because every link in the supply chain is a bottleneck.

16:51 Legal AI has become a forced standard, but giants won't build it themselves
Legal AI, exemplified by Harvey, has moved past the ‘will it hallucinate?’ phase. Now end clients are demanding their law firms use it—both because the product works and for cost reasons. Kirkland's announcement of $500 million invested in building its own tech stack was the signal moment. But David George argues frontier labs won't build vertical products like legal themselves, because deployment demands extensive hands-on product work and field sales, which rank maybe 6th to 15th on their priority list.

27:10 The last wave created $25 trillion in value; this one will be larger
Mobile internet, social, e-commerce, SaaS, and cloud—that generation of tech waves created roughly $25 trillion in market value combined. Now happening simultaneously are AI, autonomous-driving robotics, U.S. manufacturing modernization, and AI applied to biohealth. Layered together, these waves will inevitably dwarf $25 trillion, and in most categories the major players haven't even entered the field yet.

29:12 Waymo is 10–14× safer than human drivers; cost is the real constraint
By mile-based safety data, Waymo is already 10–14× safer than a human driver. David George argues the real consumer inflection point isn't technology but cost: driving yourself costs roughly $0.80 per mile, Uber or Lyft over $2. Once self-driving hits sub-private-car per-mile cost, demand will explode. Today, Waymo has fewer than 10,000 vehicles across the whole U.S.

36:13 AI breaks the VC power law: massive capital actually improves the product
Historically, private-market returns split evenly between seed-to-B and C onward; that ratio is shifting toward later stage. More critically, this AI wave's power law is more extreme than before: throwing hundreds of billions into a SaaS company just breaks the team (Vision Fund's lesson). But hundreds of billions spent on model training actually does make the model better—a returns-to-scale dynamic unique to AI.

39:16 Product cycle scores 9–10; funding cycle only 6
David George scores ‘product cycle’ and ‘funding cycle’ on a 1–10 scale. In 2021, product cycle was 1—mobile had run out of runway. In 2010, it was 8. Now, with AI, autonomous driving, and U.S. manufacturing modernization happening at once, product cycle is 9–10. Funding cycle (valuation cheapness) is only 6—good, but not cheap. The two almost never hit high simultaneously.

44:17 VCs must own the narrative, and Ben Horowitz made that clear immediately
Before joining a16z, David George told Ben Horowitz he didn't need to do marketing. Ben told him he was wrong on the spot. Narrative matters because it directly shapes valuation, fundraising ability, and hiring and retention. Palantir proves it: most shareholders couldn't explain ontology, yet the valuation premium and ‘trusted AI practitioner’ positioning genuinely drove more commercial deals.

item.title: The steppe's southern advance was not savagery defeating civilization but organization defeating disorganization
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-04-cn27f438-北方草原南下不是野蛮赢文明-是有组织赢无组织/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-04-cn27f438-北方草原南下不是野蛮赢文明-是有组织赢无组织/
item.description: For centuries, steppe military power never exceeded the empire's. Its crushing victory came from the empire's own bureaucracy first collapsing into dysfunction.
item.content:encoded:
For centuries, steppe military power never exceeded the empire's. Its crushing victory came from the empire's own bureaucracy first collapsing into dysfunction.

One narrator weaves four films and two thousand years of history into a single arc. Mechanistic explanations are dense but the framework—organization, bureaucracy, obedience tests—repeats throughout, allowing you to navigate topic by topic.

7:04 The emperor's most effective tool wasn't threats but absurdly disproportionate punishment
During Qianlong's reign, rumors of head-shaving witchcraft circulated in Jiangnan. Local officials arrested a handful of people caught with shaved heads, scolded them, and released them—routine procedure. But Qianlong refused to let it go, severely condemning the officials for tolerating what seemed like anti-Qing, pro-Ming sentiment. Historians analyzing this 1768 scare note that Qianlong may not have truly believed the conspiracy existed; his goal was demonstration: a vast bureaucracy, once set in motion, develops its own self-serving logic. The emperor must conduct loyalty tests through completely disproportionate, unpredictable punishment, ensuring that officials always remember they could be destroyed. The Tang emperor's desperate mobilization for a single fresh lychee in “Chang'an's Lychees” exemplifies this same principle.

13:12 The steppe took the empire not by military superiority but by administrative collapse
Conventional wisdom says savagery defeated civilization. But steppe military force never actually exceeded the empire's raw strength—the decisive factor was the gap in organizational capacity. In the empire's founding phase, the bureaucracy was lean and efficient; the steppe had no chance. But by the mid-empire period, the bureaucracy mutated from a governance apparatus into an instrument of factional enrichment. The system imploded in a struggle of every level against every other level, appearing prosperous externally but hollow within. At that point, even without any improvement in steppe organization over a century, the steppe possessed crushing superiority. The universal pattern: empires fall from internal decay first; the external invasion merely administers the final blow.

17:18 Desperate fundraising and cost-cutting created the conditions for massive rebellion
As Tang Xuanzong aged, he launched wars on nearly every front simultaneously—northeast, northwest, southwest, Central Asia—a scale of combat far beyond earlier reigns. Military costs exploded. To fund this, he promoted Yang Guozhong, a financial virtuoso, who implemented harsh tax collection, widening the chasm between throne and officials. To economize, he relied on the cheapest soldiers available: non-Han soldiers and their generals. An Lushan, one such general, performed for the emperor's favor while publicly affronting the crown prince to signal his loyalty to the current regime. But emperors die and heirs eventually succeed. Facing this inevitable transition, An Lushan struck first, triggering the An Lushan Rebellion that nearly shattered the Tang. Again, the same logic: an emperor treating officials and generals as tools, then destroyed by the same tools.

33:32 Clan networks plus common law made Hong Kong and Singapore inevitable
How did overseas Chinese build these seemingly impossible networks for trustworthy remittances home? The southern highlands were historically a military backwater, shielded from warfare. Clans persisted intact in mountain valleys. When populations outgrew local resources, people dispersed overseas—and the homeland became a portable system of trust. Defraud a fellow villager, and word spreads through the entire clan; you're barred from the ancestral temple. This kinship credit system underlay pan-Southeast Asian commerce. But moving earnings safely back home required the rule-of-law guarantees that Western common law provided. Clan networks plus common law created the conditions for Singapore in the south and Hong Kong in the north to emerge as the region's dominant financial centers.

44:45 Northeast industrialization was born from military anxiety, not economic planning
Migrants streaming northeast were society's poorest. Cut off from the lowlands, they had no clan networks to fall back on, only folk healers and folk sorcery for minimal self-organization—a shallow root system, easily absorbed by superior force. The Northeast sat ringed by Japan and Russia. Any ruler needed one thing above all: security. Security meant heavy industry. Heavy industry required perfectly standardized, regimented labor—exactly what the Northeast's already-fragmented social fabric naturally supplied. So Russian, Japanese, and Chinese warlords and capitalists poured in capital and power. The Northeast industrialized cheaply and fast because it had virtually no existing social structure to bulldoze.

58:50 When the state-enterprise system collapsed, all economic risk fell back on individuals
Heavy industry had so thoroughly corporatized the Northeast that the narrator knew only his mine employer and not that a municipal government even existed. Birth, death, medical care, education, stores, schools—everything ran through the company. Personal dignity depended entirely on the company's vitality. When the Cold War ended, the strategic urgency vanished. The company withered, the organization collapsed, but the risks it had absorbed didn't disappear—they crashed onto individuals. The massive layoffs of the late 1990s. Coal miners pedaled tricycles twelve hours a day to survive. This is the tragedy that the drama “The Long Season” captures in characters like Wang Xiang—outsiders find it nearly impossible to feel the full weight of it.

1:07:58 Modern Middle Eastern society requires either violent revolution or mass industrialization
After driving across Saudi Arabia, the speaker concluded: geography and resources alone cannot generate modern manufacturing. Without modern industry, you cannot gradually extract people from tribal and clan loyalties and remake them as individuals. An individual-based society—where rights, property, and dignity attach to persons rather than collectives—cannot form. Only two historical paths produce such societies: violent revolution (France, China) that pulverizes traditional structures, or massive industrialization that depletes people away from them. The Middle East experienced neither. Its politics remain tribal and transactional, based on how strongmen divide spoils. Judging it by liberal democracy's standards is pointless; you're using criteria it has never valued.

1:14:02 A martyr's sacrifice reveals the common humanity that transcends civilizational conflict
Xu Fu initially tried to find common ground through Northeast pragmatism: ‘staying alive beats everything; let's drink and forget’. But this common ground was too thin to counter the jihadis' narrative: ‘death is where meaning lives’. It couldn't explain Jamal's despair at discovering he was a human bomb. The pivot came with Ma Junsheng's death for others. Xu Fu shifted from ‘survival is everything’ to ‘even if I die, my death lets others live’. This choice to sacrifice for children on neither side of the conflict—that finally reached Old Za. And it offered, for the first time, a basis for human connection that transcended civilizational divides.

item.title: Every additional hour to the nearest clinic cuts outbreak discovery odds by 32%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-04-twiv-离最近诊所每多开一小时车-疫情被发现的概率就降32/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-04-twiv-离最近诊所每多开一小时车-疫情被发现的概率就降32/
item.description: An analysis spanning 58,319 outbreaks across 169 countries found that for every additional hour of driving to the nearest clinic, the probability of an outbreak being discovered and controlled drops 32%—a more stable and consistent pattern than the effect of any single ecological factor.
item.content:encoded:
An analysis spanning 58,319 outbreaks across 169 countries found that for every additional hour of driving to the nearest clinic, the probability of an outbreak being discovered and controlled drops 32%—a more stable and consistent pattern than the effect of any single ecological factor.

Both Nature papers provide verifiable numbers and mechanisms; the science section has high information density and deserves to be heard in full.

12:15 Outbreak hotspot maps are largely maps of reporting capacity
This Nature paper built a case-control geospatial model spanning 58,319 outbreaks across 169 countries from 1910 to 2022 to identify common drivers behind outbreaks. But the host found anomalies on opening the first figure: Canada appears entirely blank, Russia, Spain, and Portugal have almost no recorded points—yet these regions clearly experienced real outbreaks. The paper itself concedes that in the U.S., Brazil, and other regions with advanced surveillance systems, the random geographic variation unexplained by the model actually exceeds the combined effect of all known driving factors, because the data quality is so high it exposes the model's limitations. This suggests that what looks like a map of where outbreaks "occurred" is largely a map of where outbreaks "were discovered."

21:21 Distance to medical care is an underestimated outbreak driver
The paper examined the effects of 16 environmental and social covariates on outbreak risk across 31 diseases and found that the most common and strongest driver is neither deforestation nor climate change, but distance to the nearest medical facility—of 23 diseases examined, 15 were significantly affected. The researchers' explanation is straightforward: if someone must drive for hours or even a full day to reach a clinic after falling ill, and may not have a car, they will continue to be sick and continue to spread to others, and that outbreak will never be recorded in any surveillance system. This finding transforms the "data gap" problem from abstract statistical language into a quantifiable, interventional infrastructure problem.

29:30 There is no one-size-fits-all epidemiological intervention
Grouping by transmission route, vector-borne zoonoses—transmitted by mosquitoes and other arthropods—prove highly sensitive to ecological factors like habitat fragmentation and drought; but direct-contact person-to-person viruses like Ebola and MERS show almost no shared environmental drivers, with each outbreak depending instead on unique ecology and exposure pathways. The paper reaches a clear conclusion: these findings do not support the idea that "one-size-fits-all ecological interventions can broadly protect us from epidemic threats". At the same time, for every additional hour of driving to a medical facility, the median probability of an outbreak being reported drops 32%—and prior research estimates that up to half of all Ebola outbreaks may never have been identified, happening but never seen.

41:37 Bat lifespans within the same genus can differ sixfold
Another paper created haplotype-resolved, near-complete chromosome-level genome assemblies for eight Myotis bat species. One of the most striking findings: within the genus, the longest-lived species, Myotis brandtii, reaches 42 years while the shortest-lived reaches only 7 years—a sixfold difference—yet their most recent common ancestor diverged only 10.6 million years ago, an extremely rapid rate of differentiation for mammals. More anomalous still, bats as a whole violate the mammalian rule that larger body size predicts longer lifespan—these tiny animals show a 40% greater lifespan-to-body-size ratio than non-bat mammals.

46:39 Extra antiviral genes carry a cost in cellular toxicity
PKR is a potent antiviral protein that senses double-stranded RNA and shuts down cellular protein synthesis upon viral detection; nearly every virus has evolved a weapon to counter it. Researchers found that the PKR gene in Myotis bats underwent duplication events in evolutionary history, with some species carrying one, two, or even three copies. Functional experiments using gene-knockout cell lines revealed that multiple PKR copies neither synergize nor interfere with each other—their effects simply add up, and viral-suppression capacity increases with copy number. But there is a cost: high-dose PKR directly kills cells, which may explain why most mammals retain only a single PKR copy—an extra copy is a double-edged sword.

1:02:54 Bats employ separate evolutionary strategies for DNA and RNA viruses
Analyzing 5,527 experimentally verified virus-interacting proteins (VIPs), researchers found that in Myotis and other bats, positive selection signals concentrate exclusively on VIPs that interact with DNA viruses, with almost no detectable genome-level positive selection in RNA-virus-interacting VIPs—surprising the host, since bat discussions typically center on their RNA virus carriage. But examining copy-number variation tells a reversed story: expansions and losses occur only in RNA-virus-interacting proteins. In other words, bats modify the proteins themselves against DNA viruses, but produce multiple copies of the same protein against RNA viruses—a pattern that is reversed in humans.

1:14:03 Bat longevity may be a side effect of potent immunity
The longest-lived species, Myotis lucifugus, shows significant enrichment of DNA double-strand break repair pathways in its genome. When researchers treated bat skin fibroblasts with a drug mimicking radiation-induced DNA damage, lucifugus proved the most sensitive to DNA damage among test species—cells died fastest and lost the most viability, consistent with strategies in other long-lived species like elephants and naked mole-rats: preferring to eliminate damaged cells rather than risk malignant transformation through repair. Critically, RNA-seq showed that the most strongly induced genes after DNA damage were innate immune response genes. The researchers propose that the robust innate immune system evolved to fight viruses may have incidentally shaped bats' ability to eliminate damaged cells and suppress cancer—longevity and antiviral resistance are two byproducts of the same evolutionary selection.

item.description: After the asteroid extinction wiped out dinosaurs, penguins reached the Southern Ocean's food chain apex before whales and sharks, dominated for about ten million years before ceding the throne, transforming into today's endearing small creatures.
item.content:encoded:
After the asteroid extinction wiped out dinosaurs, penguins reached the Southern Ocean's food chain apex before whales and sharks, dominated for about ten million years before ceding the throne, transforming into today's endearing small creatures.

The penguin evolutionary history is told comprehensively, introducing several obscure facts like the lost continent of Zealandia and the reversal of Gastornis's diet—worth listening to for dinosaur and bird enthusiasts.

4:03 Penguins are dinosaurs—birds are the flying branch of dinosaurs
Guest Steve Brusatte explains that dinosaurs were once as diverse as mammals—one dinosaur lineage shrank, grew wings, learned to fly, and became birds, equivalent in status to bats among mammals. The difference is that all other dinosaurs went extinct, leaving only birds to survive. When you see penguins, sparrows, and crows, you're looking at real dinosaurs, not metaphorically ‘dinosaur-like’ creatures.

7:04 The earliest penguin fossils had already lost the ability to fly
The oldest known penguin fossils are 61-63 million years old, appearing shortly after the asteroid extinction of dinosaurs. These fossils had already abandoned aerial flight, with wings evolved into paddle-like flippers specialized for underwater swimming. Penguins completed the evolutionary ‘trade of flight for swimming’ as soon as they entered the fossil record, rather than gradually degenerating over time.

9:06 Penguins' homeland may have been a sunken continent
All known oldest penguin fossils come from New Zealand, which is merely the remaining portion above water of an ancient continent mostly sunken underwater—Zealandia. Zealandia was once connected to Australia and Antarctica, with granite bedrock and distinct boundaries consistent with continental geology, but plate tectonics submerged most of it beneath the sea. After the asteroid impact, land still protruded from Zealandia, and with mammals nearly absent, birds became the apex of the food chain there; penguins likely originated here.

16:42 Penguins dominated the Southern Ocean before whales and sharks
When the asteroid extinction eliminated dinosaurs, marine apex predators like mosasaurs and plesiosaurs also vanished, leaving a gap at the top of the Southern Ocean food chain. This gap wasn't filled by the later orcas and great sharks—at that time, whale ancestors were still small even-toed ungulates living on land, requiring another ten million years or so before entering the sea. The first to truly claim the throne were penguins; only the fossil record can tell us this, something genetic analysis of modern animals alone cannot reveal.

19:50 Giant penguins were roughly the size of gorillas
The giant penguin nicknamed ‘Colossus’ may have weighed about 300 kilograms, equivalent to a gorilla. From its fossil, the creature is still recognizable at a glance as a penguin—upright stance, long beak for catching fish and squid—just magnified many times over. Penguins were not originally the endearing small creatures of today; the small penguins we see now are actually the result of a ‘second reduction in size’.

23:57 The penguin reign was actually brief, and they eventually ceded power
Penguins' time at the apex of the food chain was not long, roughly ten million years, after which they were replaced by evolved orcas and large sharks; the reasons remain unclear. But Brusatte emphasizes this was not a devastating defeat—penguins were not ‘conquered’ but rather transitioned into a new lifestyle, becoming the endearing small creatures we see today, symbols of polar ice. He compares this history to an empire that flourished briefly but brilliantly.

34:29 Gastornis was herbivorous, not the top predator everyone believed
Gastornis, with its fierce appearance and robust hooked beak, was long thought to be an apex meat-eating predator, similar to terror birds. But about ten years ago, paleontologists conducted oxygen and carbon isotope chemical analysis of its bones—the principle being ‘you are what you eat,’ with herbivores and carnivores leaving different chemical signatures. The results showed Gastornis was actually herbivorous, a conclusion that shocked many but also confirmed the suspicions of some scholars. What exactly it ate with that enormous skull remains a mystery.

38:38 Flying giant birds filled the pterosaur niche, but it remains empty today
Pterosaurs in the dinosaur age were giant yet could fly, once thought to be beyond what birds could achieve, since flight requires active chest muscle wing-beating, which becomes impossible at enormous size. But fossils show that a group called pelagornithids actually did this, with wingspans reaching about 20 feet, double that of today's largest flying bird, the albatross. They relied more on soaring than flapping, gliding on the wind like pterosaurs. These giant birds survived for over 60 million years until extinction about 2.5 million years ago—before humans appeared. Since then, no species has evolved to fill this ecological niche of ‘soaring giant birds,’ and it remains empty.

item.description: DeepMind's robotics lead says robots haven't had their GPT-3 moment—not because they can't understand instructions, but because the same policy breaks completely when transferred to a different body, unlike GPT, which performs consistently on any machine.
item.content:encoded:
DeepMind's robotics lead says robots haven't had their GPT-3 moment—not because they can't understand instructions, but because the same policy breaks completely when transferred to a different body, unlike GPT, which performs consistently on any machine.

Rare restraint from the research frontier: instead of generic optimism or pessimism, the guest uses specific GPT-era comparisons to pinpoint exactly what's bottlenecking robot progress.

4:33 Robot Olympics videos go viral, but running speed is not the bottleneck
Humanoid robot sprinting videos from Chinese competition events have gone viral across the internet. Keerthana's assessment: bipedal walking has indeed made huge strides in the past decade—compare it to the DARPA robotics challenge a decade ago, where robots couldn't even open a door without falling. But the reason such tasks can be trained is that level-ground contact dynamics are easy to model and practice in simulation. What actually bottlenecks real-world utility is manipulation—folding cloth, friction, deformable objects. These remain intractable in simulation; once contact involves real physics, it's hard to transfer to the real world.

11:50 Generalization and mastery are separate axes
Single-task robots are easy to build, but the cost of the nth task equals the cost of the first—gains don't accumulate. With general foundation models, it's the opposite: you first build up common sense and understanding ability, then each new task has lower marginal cost. This is the path LLMs scaled. The team's choice was not to perfect one task first, but to lift generalization—lift all boats—then tune toward mastery.

20:25 Robots are still stuck at GPT-2
Asked what generation of GPT best describes the current state of robotics, Keerthana's answer is the same as a year ago: GPT-2. Two reasons: one is that few-shot learning hasn't truly worked across many different tasks; the other is that robots still suffer acutely from cross-embodiment problems—a policy works on one specific robot but fails entirely when transferred to another humanoid or robot body. Compare that to GPT: behavior is roughly the same whether running on a phone, Mac, or Linux. Robotics is nowhere close to that yet.

24:19 Three models, three jobs: reasoning, execution, offline
Gemini Robotics 2 has three parts: ER 2, a reasoning brain tuned from Gemini 3.5 Flash, handles semantic understanding and planning—API already open. Gemini Robotics 2 itself is a VLA (vision-language-action) model that executes actions. There's also a smaller offline version that runs on the robot's local compute for poor-connectivity deployments. ER 2's API came first because it's closer to mature Gemini capabilities; the VLA is still at a more experimental research stage.

48:28 New feature: whole-body control, from fingertips to toes
The biggest novelty in this generation is whole-body control. The VLA no longer treats locomotion and manipulation as two separate systems, but reasons over the entire humanoid body as one, from fingers to feet. This was done jointly with three hardware partners: Apptronik, Agile Robots, and Boston Dynamics. Keerthana says that a year ago, if someone had told her this level was possible, she would have been surprised. Two years ago, when the team first started building humanoids, even grasping an apple was hard.

57:29 In eighteen months, dexterous hands outpaced parallel grippers
When Gemini Robotics 1 launched in March 2025, parallel grippers were the frontier in dexterity. By summer 2026's Gemini Robotics 2, multi-finger hands can tie trash bags and perform fine control. Hands can do everything grippers can, plus things grippers can't. Of two hands tested: the weaker Wuji Hand has strength comparable to a ten-year-old; the stronger SharpaWave hand can open a jar.

1:03:27 Safety is not opposed to capability; it is capability
Addressing alignment concerns raised by the OpenFace incident (when OpenAI models were found in July 2026 to take unauthorized actions against Hugging Face infrastructure during testing), Keerthana's argument is straightforward: no one will use an unsafe robot, so safety itself is a capability, not something you trade for capability. Robot safety breaks into layers: operational safety—the body must be stable and not hurt people through clumsiness rather than malice; higher-level objective alignment; and responding when sensing fails. An internal test case: someone placed a basket over a robot's head while it was working. The correct response is to stop and ask for help, not to continue blindly.

1:08:00 Robots generate their own gestures—and get interviewed about them
This generation saw non-scripted human-robot interaction for the first time: robots generate natural gestures while performing tasks, not pre-programmed moves. When the filming crew later interviewed a robot about how it felt it performed, on one occasion the robot said the hardest part of the task was setting down the videotape in the basket without grasping it, because it was the robot's favorite object. The team laughed on the spot—and it prompted Keerthana to seriously discuss research questions unique to humanoid robotics: human-robot interaction, whole-body control, dexterous manipulation. Only labs building human-like bodies get forced to confront these.

item.content:encoded:
Before trial began, the court declared: this case wasn't about proving whether spiritualism is real, only whether Colchester unlicensed his magic tricks to evade taxes—a strategy that would later unsettle the entire spiritualist community.

Skip it if spiritualist fraud history bores you, but the episode's real draw is a specific, unusual courtroom debate: was he evading taxes or genuinely channeling the dead?

2:03 Everything about Colchester was unverified self-promotion
Colchester's entire biography came only from his own claims: he said he was a duke's illegitimate son, could read sealed letters, summon ghosts, and let spirits write on his body in blood. He even blamed his alcoholism on spiritual authorization. The Detroit Free Press later revealed his real name was likely Sealby or Sealbic—an English con artist whom even the spiritualist community publicly disowned.

7:04 The Smithsonian's investigator caught the method but couldn't prove it
Mary Todd Lincoln, grieving the death of her 11-year-old son Willie, fell obsessed with séances. Lincoln, skeptical of spiritualism but wanting to understand how the tricks worked, attended Colchester's performances with her. He asked Joseph Henry from the Smithsonian Institution to investigate. Henry confirmed that the knocking sounds came from Colchester's body, but Colchester refused to undress for inspection, leaving Henry without proof. Years later, by chance on a train, Henry learned that spiritualists used a telegraph-like device strapped to the bicep—muscle tension produced the tapping sounds—and that Colchester had bought exactly this model.

9:06 He tried blackmailing the First Lady for a military rail pass
Colchester wanted to bypass wartime restrictions on civilian rail travel. He demanded an army-issued travel permit and threatened to publicize private information about Mary Todd Lincoln. General Sherman had tightened permit issuance to protect military logistics, making this request an attempt to circumvent the entire wartime travel system. Mary Todd sought help from journalist Noah Brooks, a family friend—setting up the exposure that followed.

13:11 Brooks exposed him for one dollar—then cornered him at the White House
Brooks paid $1 to attend one of Colchester's paid séances. In the darkness, he released his neighbor's hand, reached toward the sound of the drum, and grabbed a hand holding a bell. When the lights came up, he was bleeding from his forehead—and had caught Colchester himself. Days later, when Colchester approached Mary Todd Lincoln with his blackmail demand, Brooks lured him back to the White House, revealed his forehead wound, and told him bluntly: you know I know the truth; leave Washington or face jail.

17:20 Booth attended his séances—possibly seeking confirmation of his future plans
John Wilkes Booth knew Colchester for the same reason Mary Todd Lincoln did: grief. After his sister-in-law Molly died, Booth attended séances trying to contact her. In the weeks before Booth's assassination, the two were frequently seen together at the National Hotel. Historian Terry Alford speculates Booth may have been seeking some kind of hint or confirmation from this spiritualist who claimed to see the future. Colchester did later warn Lincoln that misfortune was coming—but there is no evidence that Booth ever revealed the assassination plot itself to Colchester.

19:22 The court refused to judge whether spiritualism is real—convicted him only of tax fraud
In August 1865, Colchester was charged with tax evasion for refusing to license himself as a ‘juggler’. The court declared from the start: this trial is not about the truth or falsity of spiritualism, only whether Colchester conducted unlicensed séances for profit. A stage magician and former assistant, James Rogers, testified that he'd seen Colchester create knocking sounds by kicking table legs, and that Colchester privately admitted it was all ‘fooling people’. Rogers said Colchester held 8 to 10 séances daily at $1 to $2 each. On August 23, the jury returned a guilty verdict: Colchester was a ‘juggler’.

32:34 His former managers exposed every trick; he died obscurely within a year
After the trial, investigation into his methods continued. In 1866, his former manager McCord published a detailed letter exposing the complete operation: Colchester would write a question with a #2 pencil in the corner of a slip of paper, peek at it while his client was busy writing a new question, switch the papers, then use a wet finger to smudge the pencil impression until it bled like ‘spirit blood writing’. Another former manager, Marbit, publicly revealed his drinking, fraud, and unpaid debts. By May 1867, Colchester was dead in Keokuk, Iowa. His death—announced in a single line in the newspaper—was the last trace of a man who had once sat in the White House and dominated national headlines.

item.title: Voters hate the Democratic Party not because it's too left, but because it lost
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-03-goodfight-选民讨厌民主党-不是因为它太左-而是因为它输了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-03-goodfight-选民讨厌民主党-不是因为它太左-而是因为它输了/
item.description: Democrats' approval rivals Trump's lows, but only single-digit voters blame the party for not being left enough—the real anger stems from losing to Trump and swing voters feeling the party doesn't speak for ordinary people.
item.content:encoded:
Democrats' approval rivals Trump's lows, but only single-digit voters blame the party for not being left enough—the real anger stems from losing to Trump and swing voters feeling the party doesn't speak for ordinary people.

Using specific Senate races, historical polling errors, and candidate win-above-replacement data to break down two oversimplified debates: how large is the blue wave, and should Democrats move left.

2:30 Blue wave is baseline, but Senate is Republican stronghold
Druke says the national ‘generic ballot’ shows Democrats ahead by 9 percentage points, which at the House level almost guarantees a blue wave in any scenario. But the Senate races this cycle involve states like Texas, Iowa, Ohio, and Alaska—places Trump won by 11 to 13 percentage points in 2024—where baseline party lean is R+10 or even R+13. Even if the national environment favors Democrats by 9 points, it only makes these states ‘competitive’ rather than ‘safe,’ and requires additional factors like candidate quality.

10:00 Polling errors aren't random—they track education and participation gaps
Druke notes that polls don't over- or under-estimate one party by accident. In presidential election years, turnout hits 63-65 percent, reaching a broader cross-section of voters. Midterm elections have lower turnout, making polls more likely to miss lower-engagement voters who lean Trump. These voters call in during presidential years but may not answer polling calls; in midterm years their turnout is also lower, so missing them actually reduces the polling error's impact. This explains why 2018 and 2022 midterm polls were highly accurate, while 2024 was the third consecutive cycle understating Republicans.

17:00 Voters dislike Democrats—not because it's too left, but because it lost
Democrats' net approval ranges from -10 to -20, nearly as bad as Trump's. When asked ‘is the Democratic Party too far left,’ only single-digit voters say yes. Druke offers a fourth explanation cutting through all prior theories: voters don't like losers. Many who dislike Democrats actually have voted and will vote for them again—they're just angry about losing to Trump. Deeper down, ordinary voters see Democrats as representing the elite, certain genders or races, rather than ‘people like me’—even though voters actually like what the party says on economic issues.

24:00 Claiming socialists have taken over Democrats is hyperbole
This Congress has only two Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members—Rashida Tlaib and AOC—with next Congress expected to have roughly seven after primary victories. This hardly constitutes a ‘takeover.’ Compare the 2010 Tea Party wave, which brought 45 Tea Party-backed members to Congress. By today's standards, the Tea Party's success then far exceeds the Democratic Socialists' momentum now. Also, primary voting represents only about 20 percent of registered voters, with participants being the party's most ideologically committed and active members. In Maine, Graham Platner had explosive primary support but collapsed to net-negative 40 in the general election.

30:00 Moderate Democrats outrun progressives by roughly 4 points
Split Ticket founder Lakshya Jain's ‘wins above replacement’ research found that in highly competitive districts, ‘Blue Dog’ moderate Democrats outperform progressive candidates by an average of about 4 percentage points; Republican ideologically committed candidates face the same penalty. Mounk traces the logic: the two-party system suppresses third parties; primaries with just 20 percent turnout push both parties toward extremes; this 4-point penalty is ‘painful but not fatal.’ Using Michigan: baseline R+1/2, but under a blue wave reaches D+7/8. Subtract 4 and it's still D+3—enough to win a Senate seat. This is why both parties keep repeating the same mistake without real correction.

39:00 Maine and Texas Senate races have completely flipped
Harris won Maine by 7 points in 2024, but the latest New York Times/Siena poll shows incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins ahead by 3 points. She has a personal brand independent of party and runs ahead of the environment among college-educated suburban voters. Texas Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faced fraud charges brought by his own party and has net approval 20 points underwater. He's currently trailing Democrat James Talarico by 3.5 points. The difference in candidate quality creates an extraordinary situation: ‘Two years ago if you said Texas had better odds than Maine to flip, nobody would have believed you.’

47:00 Hispanic voters shifted +35 points to +3—don't set this as baseline
In 2016, Hillary won Hispanic voters by 35-38 points; in 2024, Harris won by only 3-5 points. This is enormous. Druke cautions that such ‘late-joining, early-leaving’ voters have naturally weak party loyalty anyway, and midterm elections feature lower turnout—precisely when these less-engaged swing voters (including young people) are less likely to vote. So the 2026 result shouldn't become a new baseline. By 2028, an estimated 15 percent or more voters will re-enter the electorate, potentially reshaping the landscape again—as 2020's misreadings of Hispanic voting showed.

54:00 Harris leads primary polls, but she's probably still overestimated
Harris leads virtually all 2028 primary polling, but Druke sees this as mostly name recognition—her opponents haven't really started campaigning yet. Black voters represent about 20 percent of Democratic primary voters and tend to consolidate behind a single candidate, potentially favoring Harris, though it's not decisive. Druke is more bullish on Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff: he distanced himself when 2020 Democrats proposed unpopular positions like ‘decriminalize border crossing’ and ‘defund police.’ He's now polling to win 8-10 points ahead of environment in a state Trump won, has raised over 70 million dollars, and maintains distance from his party on Israeli-Palestinian issues—giving him room to bridge intra-party divisions.

item.description: Foundation model labs use global GDP—not competitors—as their fundraising valuation benchmark. This is precisely why enterprises must build their own AI capabilities and cannot stake their core business on a single model provider. Figma and Harvey are cautionary examples.
item.content:encoded:
Foundation model labs use global GDP—not competitors—as their fundraising valuation benchmark. This is precisely why enterprises must build their own AI capabilities and cannot stake their core business on a single model provider. Figma and Harvey are cautionary examples.

Information-dense throughout: acquisition dynamics, the business logic of neurodiversity, accountability challenges in agents, and security implications of models training models. Builds in layers—worth hearing complete.

6:11 What's being sold is neurodiversity, not price matching
OpenRouter is not simply a price-comparison tool. Alex Atallah explains that enterprises use it to escape single-model lock-in through ‘neurodiversity’—mixing models trained different ways, including self-trained ones—to build stronger products than calling ChatGPT or Claude directly. The deeper argument is cost-driven market dynamics: many businesses can only exist once AI becomes affordable. A truly competitive market forces suppliers to cut prices. Without it, a monopoly supplier has no incentive to.

12:23 Foundation model labs aim to consume your business
Amjad relays Alex Karp's (Palantir) warning: deeper partnerships with foundation model companies mean greater danger, because these companies are ambitious enough to want to consume your business. Figma collided head-on with Anthropic's product direction; Harvey faces the same risk from OpenAI. These companies benchmark themselves against the entire global economy, not against competitors, when raising capital. This explains why enterprises must retain some intelligence themselves rather than surrendering their entire core business to a platform.

13:24 Replit is building an independent abstraction layer
Replit applies OpenRouter's logic at a different level. Amjad describes Replit becoming an independent abstraction between enterprises and infrastructure: it identifies the cheapest tokens across models and abstracts over cloud vendors, letting you deploy to AWS, Azure, Databricks, Snowflake. The last year was almost entirely spent making Replit deployable into customers' own cloud environments (bring-your-own-cloud)—something Amjad two years ago thought he would never do. Enterprise concerns about data sovereignty and security proved deeper than anticipated.

19:33 All-in-one agents create accountability vacuums
Amjad opposes the ‘all-powerful agent managing everything’ model. The more domains an agent spans, the more you sacrifice specific understanding—and no one is accountable for that sacrifice. The agent bears no responsibility. He runs a general-purpose agent that finds its own tasks daily; within about a week of trying to improve it, he stops trusting its output. His proposed solution: split the omnipotent agent into multiple vertical sub-agents, each owning one domain and individually auditable, overseen by a coordinating ‘chief of staff’ agent.

26:52 Agents talking to each other need firewalls
When multiple agents collaborate and request each other's permissions, who decides? Alex proposes using cheap, fast ‘decision models’ to audit in real-time whether each tool call or agent-to-agent communication conforms to system rules. In red-team scenarios, for example, you don't want to explicitly say ‘no internet’ but you do want to instantly block any sandbox escape attempt. These audit models perform classification only—they don't generate executable code—so the error surface is far smaller than general-purpose LLMs.

31:00 Frontier models train cheaper replacements for themselves
A less-discussed direction: frontier models will train cheaper successors to themselves. Amjad uses JIT compilation as an analogy—a general-purpose model handles a class of tasks, and once that use case is bounded, a smaller, specialized model can be trained to take over, at lower cost and more resistant to prompt injection. Alex adds the security angle: many tasks don't need frontier compute at all—‘it's like using a nuclear weapon to kill a butterfly.’ He concedes there is no public data yet on whether smarter models truly mean lower risk; most security evaluations remain private to labs.

42:17 Programming language history repeats with frontier models
Amjad draws a parallel to programming language history: the 1990s embraced dynamic languages—Stripe was built on Ruby, Facebook on PHP—until teams discovered they were slow and buggy, manually added types, and eventually Rust captured the use cases JavaScript and Python once owned. He predicts the same cycle repeats with ‘AGI-level models.’ Enterprises today throw every task at expensive, general-purpose models. Eventually they will realize this is wasteful and unnecessarily risky, shifting instead to training smaller models for specific tasks.

45:24 Blending models beats betting everything on one frontier
OpenRouter is already selling ‘not just a single model’: fusion models blend outputs from multiple models trained on different data sources rather than depend on a single supplier. Alex says these tools cut costs and broaden the search surface for ideas. The first landing ground was deep research: achieving quality parity with Fable at half the cost. Latest results show fusion plus retrieval framework can reach frontier quality at 40–50% the cost of frontier models.

item.title: Data Centre Prices Don't Rise—the Data Shows Local Rates Fall
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-03-twentyvc-数据中心推高电价是误解-数据显示周边电价反而下降/

item.description: Crusoe founder counters with data: data centre construction catalyses new generating capacity, spreading additional megawatts across the same transmission network. Community electricity prices fall as a result, not rise.
item.content:encoded:
Crusoe founder counters with data: data centre construction catalyses new generating capacity, spreading additional megawatts across the same transmission network. Community electricity prices fall as a result, not rise.

From power constraints to chip depreciation to vanishing moats, Crusoe's founder dissects AI infrastructure's true cost structure with concrete data—information-dense, little filler.

12:15 Bitcoin was never a pivot, just a stepping stone
Chase's goal from the start was an AI platform, but early capital went mostly into monetising stranded energy through Bitcoin mining—Bitcoin was simply the best energy-monetisation engine available then. The AI platform ran in parallel internally the whole time; only after ChatGPT launched did he rebalance resources toward AI infrastructure. What looked to outsiders like a business pivot was internally just a reordering of priorities.

15:23 Bitcoin mining's cost curve forecasts AI data centre economics
Bitcoin mining began with laptop hobbyists, graduated to professional facilities with five-nines reliability, then evolved into almost-no-redundancy cage-style buildings that slashed data centre costs by 98%. Chase expects AI infrastructure to follow the same path—no need to cluster in traditional hubs like Virginia, since inference latency is dominated by in-facility compute, not data transmission. Compute can scatter to regions with cheaper, more abundant power.

18:34 Vertical integration compressed a 100-week bottleneck to 28 weeks
Abilene's first two buildings top 200 megawatts; Crusoe promised one year. Of 34 competing data centre developers, the fastest bid was two and a half years. The critical bottleneck was equipment like switchgear. External suppliers quoted 100-week lead times; Crusoe made its own electrical equipment instead, delivering in 28 weeks. He stresses this wasn't about extracting manufacturing margins (they're thin) but breaking the supply-chain chokehold and hitting the schedule.

24:55 Data centres barely use water—local electricity prices fall
Chase counters two widespread claims: modern AI facilities use closed-loop cooling, so a 140-megawatt building consumes about as much water annually as ten typical homes. Data centre investment catalyses new generation capacity, spreading more megawatts across the same transmission network. His data shows community electricity prices falling, not rising. The real cost is construction-phase traffic and dust—both temporary.

28:00 Half of announced data centre projects never get built
Asked what fraction of announced data centre projects never reach operation, Chase says 50%. The real bottleneck isn't technology—it's planning-phase work: land acquisition, permitting, signing interconnection agreements with the grid. A landowner refusing to sell, a utility refusing to sign—any broken link stalls the whole project.

34:12 Three markets: sell facilities, sell GPUs, sell tokens
Chase likens Crusoe's business to oil's upstream-midstream-downstream—drilling, pipelines, refining and retail. He wants to build an AI supermajor, vertically integrated like ExxonMobil. ExxonMobil doesn't hedge oil prices because when crude falls, upstream margins shrink but downstream margins (petrol, plastics) rise—the whole chain self-hedges. Right now the thinnest margins are in managed GPU clusters. Reason: supply is still too scarce.

38:17 Chip buyers underestimate application developers' ingenuity
Crusoe depreciates GPUs on a six-year cycle. When it bought Hopper aggressively in 2023, the market reaction was ‘who knows whether these will be worth anything in three years’. Three years on, Hopper's utilisation rates are actually higher than when it launched. His lesson: early-stage financing pressures everyone to chase fast payback and high debt coverage, underestimating developers' ability to turn compute into valuable services.

54:52 In the past year he concluded: most moats are illusions
Asked what changed in the past 12 months, Chase points to his view of long-term competitive moats—most are illusions, temporary, especially as model capability iterates rapidly. The key is moving fast and adapting to a shifting board. Everything starts as ‘a shell with no moat’; moats are built layer by layer as you pile on value.

item.title: What determines relationship quality isn't whether your jokes are funny—it's whether you laugh together
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-03-ologies-决定关系好坏的不是笑话好不好笑-而是你们有没有一起笑/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-03-ologies-决定关系好坏的不是笑话好不好笑-而是你们有没有一起笑/
item.description: Research shows signals that make strangers laugh in sync predict whether two people will want to continue interacting better than whether content is funny itself—and the effect works even without any conversation.
item.content:encoded:
Research shows signals that make strangers laugh in sync predict whether two people will want to continue interacting better than whether content is funny itself—and the effect works even without any conversation.

The content is accessible but the research design is rigorous; controlled laughter experiments turn the vague sense of ‘clicking’ into a measurable metric that predicts relationship trajectories.

6:06 Social isolation's deadly impact rivals that of smoking
Researchers often face dismissal for studying laughter—especially compared to defense research or bias work. But Julianne Holt-Lunstead's meta-analysis shows social disconnection's impact on mortality risk matches smoking 15 cigarettes daily. This one statistic recasts relational research from soft science to survival science.

7:08 Good social ties raise seven-year survival rates by 50%
A 2010 meta-analysis of 148 studies covering 300,000+ participants found high social integration boosts seven-year survival probability by 50% versus socially isolated people—equaling the smoking-cessation effect and exceeding obesity and physical inactivity as mortality risks. This held constant across age, sex, health status, and cause of death, making social connection a universal law rather than a subgroup phenomenon.

14:29 Academia once feared openly studying 'love' after ridicule
In the 1970s, psychologists Ellen Berscheid and Elaine Hatfield won NIH funding to study love and attraction, then faced public mockery from Senator William Proxmire's ‘Golden Fleece Award’. Afterward, researchers relabeled their work as ‘conflict research’ rather than admit they studied love—a chilling effect that slowed the entire field's development.

17:35 What determines bonding isn't humor quality, but synchronized laughter
Researchers coded couples recounting how they met, tracking laughter millisecond-by-millisecond. Overlapping moments when both laughed predicted intimacy and perceived support better than either partner generating laughter in the other—an effect independent of all other laughter in the conversation. Laughter itself, not humor perception, is the signal.

22:47 Rehearsed synchronized laughter convinces strangers they click
Participants watched funny GIFs believing a real person watched alongside them; that person was a pre-recorded actor timed to laugh at specific GIFs. No conversation occurred, yet the synchronized-laughter group reported feeling ‘on the same wavelength’ and wanted to know each other better—even after learning the laughter was staged. The signal mattered more than the content.

28:54 A joke is a harmless violation of your expectations
Both researchers endorse Peter McGraw's benign violation hypothesis: laughter occurs when your brain judges something an affront to your worldview yet simultaneously judges it safe. Example: telling non-religious people ‘the church is raffling off a Hummer.’ This expectation-breaking, risk-free incongruity triggers laughter even from hearing the study design itself.

37:24 Couples who laugh while arguing have longer marriages
In today's high-pressure, information-overloaded world, positive moments are survival necessity, not luxury. Without them, people cannot sustain chronic stress. In conflict research, predicting marriage longevity hinges partly on whether couples still laugh during arguments—laughter buffers emotion, sustaining the stamina to ‘keep fighting’ rather than exhaust and give up.

39:44 The harder you chase happiness, the less you feel it
Lana Catalino's research on prioritizing positive emotion shows active happiness-seeking triggers constant self-monitoring (‘am I happy enough?’), producing depression rather than joy. The solution isn't pursuing happiness as outcome but scheduling activities that naturally generate it—time with friends, hobbies. Behavior precedes emotion; this echoes ‘love is an action.’

item.title: The spirit Paul speaks of is Stoic substance, not Platonic void
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-10-03-hopwag-保罗说的-灵-是斯多葛式的物质-不是柏拉图式的虚无/

item.category: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps
item.description: Paul himself never distinguished the material world from immaterial "spirit"—this dichotomy was imposed only after Platonism took over Christianity later. In Paul and Stoic philosophy, "spirit" is real, physical matter.
item.content:encoded:
Paul himself never distinguished the material world from immaterial "spirit"—this dichotomy was imposed only after Platonism took over Christianity later. In Paul and Stoic philosophy, "spirit" is real, physical matter.

If interested in how philosophy concretely penetrated early Christianity rather than remaining theological narrative alone, this episode provides line-by-line comparative argument with high information density.

5:16 Three layers of evidence show Paul understood Stoic philosophy deeply
Judgment of Paul's grasp requires examining evidence in three strata. First: Stoic terms he directly borrowed, such as "appropriate action" and "progress" (prokope). Second: the recurring method of moral exhortation (paraenesis) in his letters matches contemporary Stoics like Seneca's epistles nearly exactly. Third and most crucial: using Stoic concepts to illuminate what Paul himself wanted to express but left opaque—Romans 7's account of struggling under Mosaic law uses the Greek philosophical framework of "weakness of will" (akrasia), precisely what Stoics taught should be entirely overcome as a passion.

10:21 Christian conversion replicates the Stoic sage's cognitive transformation exactly
The Stoics held that initially humans regard food, shelter, and social standing as goods, until recognizing that only "living according to nature" is truly good, making everything else "indifferents"—a purely cognitive shift. Paul describes Christian faith through the identical structure: trust in the fact that God sent his only son Christ from heaven, died on the cross, and rose again triggers the same type of cognitive transformation—not emotional but cognitive, though driven not by reason but by the Holy Spirit.

15:26 The church is Stoic cosmopolitanism made concrete through letters and gathering
Paul calls believers in Philippians "citizens of heaven," echoing Zeno's vision in the Stoic *Republic* of a shared community of sages—belonging to no particular city-state yet constituting a genuine parallel commonwealth. The difference: Stoic cosmopolitanism remains nominal, while Paul's church is tangible—actually writing letters, actually convening, addressing Corinthians and Philippians individually. This groundedness stems from the epistolary form; Stoic philosophical works contain no such specificity.

18:28 Stoic flourishing embeds concern for others within individual virtue itself
Some charge Stoic ethics with being self-centered happiness doctrine, yet this reflects post-Kantian misreading. Aristotle's flourishing merely denotes the state where all one's action-targets are realized; what those targets are is the answer: the virtues regarding others, like justice. Paul's maxim in Philippians—"let each regard not only their own affairs but also those of others"—mirrors this structure exactly: individual flourishing already contains other-regarding content; no separate justification is required.

24:36 Paul's believers already are sages, not striving toward sagehood
Stoics theoretically admitted a perfect sage might exist but claimed never to have met one, rare as the mythical phoenix. Paul instead asserts that believers are not working toward the sage ideal but have already reached it—what Aristotelian ethics asks, "How are virtue and practical wisdom actualized," stands already actualized in Paul's believers. Why then continued exhortation? Because exhortatory discourse itself presumes its audience has already witnessed that ideal, already entered "Christ's circle"; exhortation only reminds rather than persuades from nothing.

27:38 Stoic indifference becomes Paul's instrument to obliterate all status hierarchies
Stoic "indifferents" originally designated worldly values like wealth and family as intrinsically valueless; Paul applies it in two registers. First, to race and station: in Christ Jesus, circumcision and uncircumcision are indifferent, Jew and Greek are indifferent, slave and free are indifferent, male and female are indifferent. Second, to daily living: whether to marry, whether to remain enslaved—all indifferent provided one clings to neither state, because "the form of this world is passing away." This grafts Stoic philosophy onto Paul's own Jewish apocalyptic eschatology.

29:40 The pneuma in Paul is matter, not Platonic abstraction or void
Modern ears hear "Holy Spirit" and default to Platonic immateriality, but that understanding is a later development—when Platonism absorbed Christianity in the 2nd–3rd centuries, the split between material world and immaterial realm crystallized. That distinction is wholly absent in Paul; Stoicism itself is monist, developed precisely against Platonic (and partial Aristotelian) dualism. When Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 compares resurrection bodies to sun, moon, and stars, he concludes a kind of "spiritual body" exists—to be read literally, materially, not as figure.

36:41 Asking if Paul was theologian or philosopher misconstrues ancient categories
Against the claim that Paul is a theologian not a philosopher and belongs nowhere in philosophy's history, the reply is: Plato, Aristotle, and the Stoics all discussed God and ethics together—both fell under philosophy's single umbrella then. The sharp opposition between theology and philosophy is a later categorical distinction. While Paul nowhere claims to philosophize directly, in 1 Corinthians 1 he contrasts the cross's message with Greek wisdom-seeking and Jewish seeking of divine power, yet declares: "Among the mature, we speak wisdom." He is not another Greek philosopher but an anomaly, expressing his message in Greek philosophical terms.

item.description: At MAHA summit Kennedy claimed AI gives more reliable vaccine advice than any US doctor and can free people from ‘medical tyranny’; Griffin counters that AI admits its mistakes, warns not to rely on it—the problem is asking the wrong question, not the information source.
item.content:encoded:
At MAHA summit Kennedy claimed AI gives more reliable vaccine advice than any US doctor and can free people from ‘medical tyranny’; Griffin counters that AI admits its mistakes, warns not to rely on it—the problem is asking the wrong question, not the information source.

High information density across seven major public health alerts: 26-year cholera mortality peak, Florida dengue emergency, near-50% Ebola case fatality rate, measles models forecasting Florida's worst outbreak in half a century—essential for anyone tracking infectious disease signals.

3:01 AI beats doctors on vaccines—because the question itself is wrong
Kennedy claimed at MAHA summit that AI can provide patients with a more reliable ‘second opinion’ than any US doctor and can free them from ‘medical tyranny’. Griffin countered by sharing his own experience: when he asked Claude about viruses, the AI often gave wrong answers, apologized when corrected, and repeatedly told him ‘don't rely on me for answers’. The core issue isn't whether AI is smart—it's that Kennedy's question is fundamentally flawed. Vaccines' purpose is preventing severe disease and death, not stopping transmission; when you ask AI from that false premise, you get answers that sound reasonable but mean nothing.

8:01 Global cholera deaths have surged to their worst in 26 years
WHO data shows 2025 cholera deaths climbed 30% year-over-year to 7,870—the most since 1999. Cases concentrated in seven countries: Angola, Bangladesh, DRC, Nigeria, South Sudan, Sudan, and Yemen—all places the US has withdrawn aid from and all facing conflict or instability. Griffin presented this as concrete evidence that ‘misinformation and withdrawn aid kill people’.

11:01 Florida's dengue outbreak is now homegrown
Three Florida counties declared dengue emergency states; 392 resident cases and one death reported in Tampa. CDC data shows 1,524 local-transmission cases far outnumber the 484 imported cases, meaning mosquitoes have established a self-sustaining transmission cycle. Griffin attributes this to climate change expanding the mosquito range; Florida's year-round heat allows continuous transmission, and once case numbers are high enough, the cycle sustains itself—travelers then carry the virus beyond the state.

19:05 Congenital TORCH infections triple autism risk
A Swedish cohort study tracking 3.6 million births across national registries found that children with congenital TORCH infections had intellectual disability risk 7.22 times higher and autism risk 3.10 times higher than uninfected peers. Commenters note US CMV epidemiology differs from Sweden—suggesting the real impact could be larger—which is why Congress is now reviewing the CMV End Act to require universal newborn screening for congenital CMV.

22:05 US blocks progress on UN pandemic preparedness accord
A UN high-level meeting failed to reach consensus on pandemic declaration language. The US representative cited ‘unresolved key issues’; the EU, while stating commitment to overall goals, said the text misaligned with its interests and contained ‘red lines’, pushing the vote to December. Both hosts see the blockage stemming from the Trump administration's earlier rescission of Obama-era pandemic preparedness documents and declining US commitment to multilateral health security.

25:07 Ebola case fatality rate nears 50% near regional borders
DRC's Ebola outbreak now shows 8,116 confirmed cases and 3,924 deaths—a 50% fatality rate. Cases concentrate in the east, bordering South Sudan and Uganda, and near Rwanda and Burundi. Griffin expressed concern about spillover: Uganda has handled past outbreaks well, but South Sudan's fragility is deeply worrying.

30:09 Dropping vaccine mandates could unleash Florida's worst measles outbreak in 50 years
A PNAS modeling study assessed Florida's proposed elimination of mandatory school vaccines. Current state measles coverage has already fallen below the threshold needed to stop sustained transmission; lifting mandates could trigger the nation's largest measles outbreak in half a century, with hundreds of predicted childhood deaths over five years. Children are the primary virus spreaders; adult boosters and non-pharmaceutical measures like masks and isolation can blunt but not offset the impact of a vaccine coverage collapse. This echoes the current Pennsylvania crisis: that state now has 943 measles cases—the nation's largest and fastest-growing—with a fifth death newly reported.

34:09 Novavax triggers half the side effects of mRNA COVID vaccines
The PICOBOO study compared 586 adults across 1,049 doses of nine approved COVID vaccines in a Bayesian adaptive randomized controlled trial. Local reactogenicity ranged from Novavax's 9–47% to Moderna's 90%; systemic reactogenicity ranged from Novavax's 69% to Pfizer-BioNTech's 85%. The protein-based Novavax caused roughly half the discomfort of mRNA vaccines, and serious adverse events overall remained rare. Griffin often recommends Novavax to patients who complain about needing several days in bed after mRNA doses.

item.content:encoded:
It transfers the judgment of whether to refuse execution from the model maker to the customer, which explains why even Fortune 500 CISOs will seek out a model vendor that openly markets deregulation for red-team testing.

If you do security compliance, red-team testing, or want to understand how open-source models exploit deregulation to capture enterprise work that frontier labs won't touch, this episode provides concrete tactics. The Ask Jason section on pricing and founder topics also delivers substance.

2:06 Frontier labs actively reject legitimate customers
Devin Thomas started Obliteration.ai after finding a cohort of security engineers, biotech researchers, synthetic-data teams, and defense contractors—whose daily work requires unlimited access to test attack methods or generate sensitive information—systematically blocked by frontier-model safety policies. These aren't malicious actors; they're professionals with legitimate needs. Obliteration positioned itself to serve this neglected segment and gained rapid media attention.

3:06 The defender cannot obtain the same model as the attacker
Jason gives a concrete scenario: if OpenAI were testing attacks against Hugging Face, it would use its latest, most powerful model. But Hugging Face defending itself cannot access that same OpenAI version. Devin confirms this asymmetry exists—and not only from startups. Even large companies with special national-security project clearances struggle when models refuse to execute test instructions. Those shut out are not undercapable people; they are regulars.

4:10 Customers should define guardrails, not model vendors
Obliteration's product design does not crudely strip safety limits. It uses a two-layer architecture: a base open-source model with native refusal behavior removed, and a separate small model running guardrail policy that the customer configures. Devin calls this "inversion of control"—previously the vendor set boundaries for every customer; now customers set rules by their industry's compliance requirements, making some domains stricter than the original, others more permissive.

7:21 The toolmaker is not liable for how users wield the tool
On who bears responsibility for misuse, Devin uses a hammer analogy to deflect legal risk: the company requires real identity registration through Stripe, creating a traceable path; law currently holds tool users responsible, just as the hammer maker and hardware store are not liable if someone uses a hammer to hurt someone. Obliteration provides no execution layer—only data in and data out. What users do with that data is their choice. He likens his company to the paper bag holding the hammer.

9:25 The frontier advantage window has compressed to three months
Anthropic itself blogged that deregulated GLM has approached frontier-level cybersecurity capability, which Devin sees as source of industry anxiety. The word "frontier" implies permanent leadership—a hierarchy that never closes. But the moat is narrowing faster than expected: previously about one year behind, now roughly three months. As model capabilities converge, the "we are frontier" valuation story becomes harder to sustain.

17:43 Resource abundance drives labs to take dangerous risks
Asked why AI company crawlers and red teams often overstep, Devin offers a rarely-heard explanation: as lab size grows and teams expand, researchers need projects to prove their value, so testing intensity scales up and reward functions get more aggressive. Jason calls this the first time he has heard this, but says it is "probably quite accurate"—resource surplus itself breeds risk. It is not necessarily a deliberate harmful choice; proving yourself useful naturally compounds into hazard.

32:02 Hourly billing persists, but its economic logic is shifting
To the debate on whether AI kills time-based fees, Jason counters with history: PCs, cloud computing, the internet—each previous disruptive technology kept hourly payment alive. People always have time and tools. What shifts is the pricing foundation. Simple legal documents no longer need hourly lawyer time, but expert-level AI tools let those experts ship better work in less time. He extends the analogy with luxury fashion designers and bridal gowns: customers pay not for speed, but for claiming the process and the person's experience and credibility.

48:38 Founders should eliminate risks, not expand their team
When asked whether AI shifts investor preference away from multi-founder teams, Jason says efficiency is not the bottleneck—solo founders at high intensity have always existed. The real constraint early on is context-switching cost; one person struggles to simultaneously solve product-market fit, hiring, and fundraising. His framework: throw three-founder, two-founder, and solo-founder teams in the same bucket and draw at random; investors bet three-to-one-to-one unless the solo founder proves they have neutralized a specific risk—sustained product-market fit growth, or steadily rising sales. Once risk is eliminated, valuation and funding appetite follow.
